# Anamatagga Saṁyutta (SN 15)

**ID:** SN 15
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Anamatagga Saṁyutta
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0302m.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Anamatagga Saṁyutta* (SN 15) is the fifteenth chapter of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Nidānavagga* [Bodhi 2003]. It comprises twenty discourses organized into two chapters (*vagga*s) [Hazra 1994]. Its unifying theme is the fathomless, unbounded temporal extent of rebirth (*saṁsāra*), countering mythological creation narratives by emphasizing that the ultimate beginning of existence cannot be discerned or known [Bodhi 2003; Nyanatiloka 1938]. The core homily repeated throughout the collection declares that for beings hindered by ignorance and bound by craving who roam and wander on, no prior limit (*pubbā koṭi*) is known [Shenghai Li 2012; Bodhi 2003]. The Buddha illustrates this vast duration through evocative similes, including mountains of bones left by a single person over eons, tears wept in grief, and maternal milk consumed across successive lifetimes.

The title term *anamatagga* has attracted extensive philological and doctrinal analysis. The commentary (*Sāratthappakāsinī*) resolves it as *anu-amatagga*, glossing that even if one pursues the beginning through knowledge (*ñāṇena anugantvā*) for centuries or millennia, it remains unthought-of and undiscoverable (*amatagga* / *aviditagga*) [Silk 2015; Bodhi 2003]. Its Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit counterpart is *anavarāgra* ("without lower or upper limit"), with cognates in Prakrit (e.g. Ardhamāgadhī *aņavadagga*) and Chinese translations rendering it as "without beginning" (*wushi*) or "without limit" [Silk 2015; Shenghai Li 2012]. In Theravāda historical chronicles, the *Anamatagga Saṁyutta* is remembered as the sermon delivered by the elder Rakkhita to convert the region of Vanavāsa after the Third Council [Gombrich et al. 1994; Buswell & Lopez 2014]. In northern scholasticism, the sutta's opening passage was frequently cited by Madhyamaka commentators—including Qingmu, the *Akutobhayā*, Buddhapālita, and Candrakīrti's *Prasannapadā*—to debate the reality versus emptiness of *saṁsāra* [Shenghai Li 2012].

**Sources**

- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha (2003) — Described position within the Nidānavagga, translation of the title, core doctrine of saṁsāra, and commentary on anamatagga and anavarāgra.
- [Shenghai Li 2012] Shenghai Li, Candrakīrti’s Āgama: A Study of the Concept and Uses of Scripture in Classical Indian Buddhism (2012) — Detailed the opening doctrinal formula, Chinese Samyuktāgama parallels, Sanskrit title variants, and citation by Madhyamaka commentators.
- [Silk 2015] Jonathan A. Silk, Buddhist Cosmic Unity (2015) — Provided linguistic analyses of anamatagga, Prakrit forms, and Buddhaghosa's commentary on SN 15.1.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Confirmed the structure of twenty discourses in two chapters.
- [Nyanatiloka 1938] Nyanatiloka Mahāthera, Guide Through the Abhidhamma Piṭaka (1938) — Noted the Buddha's refutation of an absolute primeval beginning in the Anamatagga Saṁyutta.
- [Gombrich et al. 1994] Richard Gombrich et al., King Asoka and Buddhism: Historical and Literary Studies (1994) — Documented the tradition that Rakkhita preached the Anamatagga Saṁyutta in Vanavāsa.
- [Buswell & Lopez 2014] Robert E. Buswell Jr. and Donald S. Lopez Jr., Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism (2014) — Corroborated Rakkhita's mission to Vanavāsi preaching the Anamatagga Saṁyutta.
